channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Austria's record drought has caused around EUR 1bn in farm damage and forced early cattle slaughter, while low water on the Rhine has cut barge capacity to about 20% — underscoring climate-driven supply-chain risk in Europe.
item.description:
Austria's hail insurer put drought-related farm damage at about EUR 1bn as of 10 August, with cattle farms hit hardest as grassland and fodder yields fall by up to half, pushing some to cull livestock early. In Germany, persistent low water on the Rhine has cut the load some operators can carry to roughly 20% of normal, forcing freight onto trucks that cannot fully absorb the volume — a shift commentators tie directly to climate change and warn will raise prices. At the same time, storms with heavy rain flooded parts of Bavaria, showing the swing between drought and extreme rainfall.

Industry Impact

The Rhine is a critical artery for moving chemical feedstocks and finished products in Europe, so repeated low-water episodes disrupt inbound raw materials and outbound shipments and raise logistics costs for chemical and ACS producers with German and Central European operations. Drought and volatile weather also pressure agricultural feedstock availability and prices for bio-based inputs. The recurring pattern argues for building water-level contingencies into European logistics planning rather than treating each drought as a one-off.

Rinderzucht Austria | WirtschaftsWoche | Süddeutsche Zeitung

item.title: Shanghai cut minimum second-home down-payments to 15% in the suburbs and added trade-in and voucher incentives from 21 August, and issued a 15th Five-Year Plan for urban renewal and housing.
item.description:
Six Shanghai departments announced eight measures to revive the property sector: the minimum down-payment on suburban second homes drops from 20% to 15% (25% inside the outer ring), alongside second-hand-home acquisition support, housing vouchers, "trade-in" purchase subsidies and easier provident-fund withdrawals, effective 21 August. Shanghai also released its 15th Five-Year Plan for urban renewal and housing development, with 23 key tasks and 19 indicators aimed at a "new development model" for real estate by 2030. Separately, an industry report set out the medium-to-long-term path for China's power-construction sector, including ultra-high-voltage lines, grid upgrades and smart microgrids.

Industry Impact

Construction and real estate are among the largest end-markets for adhesives, coatings and sealants, so measures to stabilise Chinese property demand directly affect volumes for construction chemicals. The emphasis on urban renewal and renovation (rather than only new build) points demand toward repair, retrofit and refurbishment products. The power-construction and grid-upgrade pipeline adds a durable infrastructure demand stream for protective coatings and sealants. These are signals of where China's construction-linked ACS demand will concentrate over the coming plan period.

Xinhua | China Economic Net | China Economic Net

item.title: Anutin Charnvirakul's Bhumjaithai Party won over 190 seats in Thailand's election, making him the first premier re-elected in nearly 20 years, while Thai Q2 GDP grew 1.9% and Indonesia expanded 5.45% in the first half.
item.description:
Thailand's snap election delivered a clear winner: Bhumjaithai, led by Anutin Charnvirakul, took more than 190 seats, strengthening his mandate and making him the first Thai prime minister re-elected after a general election in almost two decades. The economic backdrop is mixed: Thailand's second-quarter GDP grew 1.9% year-on-year but fell 0.2% from the prior quarter, with analysts at KResearch warning that much of the beat came from inventory build-up rather than durable demand. Indonesia, by contrast, grew 5.45% in the first half (5.29% in Q2) and is pushing downstream-processing projects toward an 8% growth target.

Industry Impact

Southeast Asia is a growth region for construction, automotive and consumer manufacturing that use adhesives, coatings and sealants, so political stability in Thailand plus solid Indonesian growth support the demand outlook and investment case there. The contrast between soft Thai momentum and stronger Indonesian expansion helps prioritise where to focus commercial effort. Indonesia's downstream-industrialisation drive — refining, minerals processing, waste-to-energy — points to specific project pipelines where industrial coatings and sealants demand will build.

Lianhe Zaobao | The Nation | Kompas

item.title: The US added 43 Chinese companies to its import blacklist in late July over alleged forced labour in Xinjiang, though local processors report the region's cotton-textile supply chain is still booming, with processing rates around 30–40%.
item.description:
Washington expanded its Xinjiang-related import restrictions, adding 43 Chinese firms in late July under forced-labour allegations tied to the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. Such listings bar the named companies' goods from entering the US unless importers can prove they are free of forced labour. Despite the measure, a cotton-ginning mill owner in southern Xinjiang told reporters that local cotton processing rates are running at about 30–40% and that the wider textile supply chain continues to expand, suggesting domestic and non-US demand is absorbing the output.

Industry Impact

For chemical and ACS producers the direct exposure is limited, but the mechanism matters: US forced-labour import bans keep widening and can catch any supplier whose inputs trace back to listed Chinese entities or regions. This raises the compliance burden on supply-chain due diligence and traceability, particularly for textiles, agriculture-linked inputs and any materials sourced through Xinjiang. It is another data point in the steady decoupling of US and Chinese supply chains that ACS companies must map across their own customer and supplier networks.

South China Morning Post

item.title: Unitree Robotics debuted on Shanghai's STAR Market up about 460% at a CNY 342bn valuation, as China shipped over 40,000 humanoid robots in H1 2026 — about 97% of the global total — and sector revenue rose 24.5%.
item.description:
Unitree (also reported as Yushu Technology), billed as China's first humanoid-robot stock, opened up 629% and closed 460% above its issue price, reaching a market value near CNY 342bn. Industry data released around the 2026 World Robot Conference in Beijing showed China shipped more than 40,000 humanoid robots in the first half — about 97% of the global total — with domestic core-component localisation above 75%. First-half revenue for larger robot firms rose 24.5% to CNY 165.5bn, and shipments are forecast at 38,000 units for the full year 2026, rising to 380,000 by 2030. Demonstrations featured robots running full warehouse logistics workflows.

Industry Impact

The robotics build-out is both a customer and a competitive-context signal. Automated assembly and warehouse robots expand demand for specialised adhesives, coatings and sealants used in robot manufacturing and in the electronics inside them. More broadly, rapid Chinese automation lowers manufacturing labour costs and strengthens China's position across the industrial supply chains that ACS producers serve. The concentration of shipments and component localisation in China also indicates where future automation-driven materials demand — and competition — will be centred.

Xinhua Daily | Global Times | China Economic Net

item.title: Japan's July exports rose 23.2% year-on-year, core inflation held at 1.8%, and the flash manufacturing PMI climbed to 55.1 in August, reinforcing expectations of a September rate rise to 1.25%.
item.description:
The data pointed to steady momentum. July exports grew 23.2%, beating forecasts and extending gains to eleven months, driven by electronic components and semiconductor manufacturing equipment; imports rose 27.8% as Japan sought new crude supplies amid the Hormuz disruption. Core CPI (which includes energy but excludes fresh food) rose 1.8%, still below the Bank of Japan's 2% target for a seventh month, held down by fuel subsidies but lifted by firms passing on higher import costs and a weak yen. The flash August manufacturing PMI — where readings above 50 signal expansion — rose to 55.1 from 54.5. Markets widely expect the BOJ to raise rates from 1% to 1.25% on 17–18 September.

Industry Impact

Japan is both a major chemical producer and a key export market, so firm factory activity and rising new orders support industrial demand for coatings, adhesives and sealants tied to electronics, autos and machinery. A likely BOJ hike and a still-weak yen shape currency exposure and the relative cost of Japanese versus imported materials. Rising input costs feeding into consumer prices confirm that raw-material inflation is being passed along the chain — relevant when negotiating pricing with Japanese customers and suppliers.

Il Sole 24 Ore | Channel News Asia | MarketScreener

item.title: Switzerland and China concluded an upgraded free-trade deal giving 99.8% of Swiss exports duty-free access, while the India–EU pact cleared legal scrubbing for likely signature in 2026 with duty-free access for 93% of Indian shipments.
item.description:
Two large trade blocs moved forward at once. Switzerland and China finished negotiating an updated FTA on 20 August that lifts duty-free coverage for Swiss exports to 99.8% from roughly half under the 2014 deal, benefiting watches, pharmaceuticals and precision instruments and adding stricter labour and environmental provisions; signing is planned before end-2026. Separately, the EU and India completed the legal review of their trade-pact text, with signature expected in 2026; the deal would give 93% of Indian shipments duty-free EU access and cheaper EU cars and wine into India. Together the EU and India represent about a quarter of global GDP.

Industry Impact

Both deals lower tariff barriers in markets that matter to chemical and adhesives trade flows and reshape competitive positioning. Easier China access for Swiss and European specialty producers can help exporters, while an India–EU deal opens a large, fast-growing market and could shift where European chemical majors invest and source. For ACS producers, the practical takeaways are new duty-free lanes to factor into pricing and sourcing, and the reminder that these modern deals bundle in labour and environmental rules that affect compliance, not just tariffs.

The Straits Times | Asharq Al-Awsat | The Economic Times

item.title: A senior AECC engineer said China aims to replace imported paints, sealants, rubber, bolts and cleaning agents on its C919 narrowbody airliner with locally-made products to cut geopolitical and supply-chain exposure, with 42 C919s delivered by July 2026.
item.description:
Zhang Xiaoyan, a chief engineer at the Aero Engine Corporation of China's Beijing Institute of Aeronautical Materials, said the country is working to localise the materials that go into its passenger aircraft, singling out paints, sealants, rubber, bolts and cleaning agents for the C919. The stated aim is to reduce dependence on Western suppliers amid geopolitical and supply-chain pressure. Comac had delivered 42 C919s to domestic customers by July 2026, and the localisation drive is not expected to derail the aircraft's bid for EU safety approval.

Industry Impact

This is a direct competitive signal for the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) industry: aerospace paints, sealants and specialty adhesives are high-value, high-specification products, and China is explicitly working to substitute imports with domestic alternatives in a flagship programme. In the near term the C919 volumes are small, but the intent points to a shrinking addressable market for Western aerospace ACS suppliers in China over time, and to a domestic Chinese capability in qualified aerospace-grade sealants and coatings that could later compete elsewhere. Suppliers should watch which materials get localised first and how fast qualification proceeds.

South China Morning Post

item.title: China's Ministry of Commerce confirmed anti-dumping duties on imported copolymer polyoxymethylene (POM), a common engineering plastic, with Daicel inheriting Polyplastics' 35.5% and 3.8% rates from 21 August.
item.description:
POM (polyoxymethylene, or polyformaldehyde copolymer) is an engineering plastic used in precision parts across autos, electronics and consumer goods. In May 2025 China imposed five-year anti-dumping duties — extra import taxes meant to counter below-cost pricing — on POM from the US, EU, Taiwan and Japan, at rates up to 35.5%. After a corporate reorganisation, Daicel Corporation applied to take over Polyplastics' business; on 20 August the Ministry of Commerce approved Daicel Corporation inheriting the 35.5% rate and Daicel's Taiwan unit the low 3.8% rate, effective 21 August. Exports shipped under the old Polyplastics Taiwan name instead face 32.6%.

Industry Impact

This is a concrete signal for the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) industry on how China now polices imported specialty chemicals and polymers: anti-dumping duties on a specific material can be maintained through corporate restructurings, and the applicable rate depends on the exact legal entity and name on the shipment. For any ACS or chemical producer selling engineering polymers or specialty inputs into China, it underlines the need to track duty scope and to confirm which corporate entity is on the paperwork, since the wrong name here means a nearly tenfold jump in duty (3.8% to 32.6%).

China Economic Net | China Daily | Chinatimes

item.title: A Strategy& study found German automotive suppliers' global market share fell to 23% in 2025 from 26% a decade earlier, while Chinese suppliers nearly tripled to 14% and earned far higher profit per employee.
item.description:
The consulting firm Strategy& reports a steady erosion of Germany's supplier base. Global share dropped to 23% from 26% ten years ago, while Chinese suppliers rose from 5% to 14%. Profitability has diverged sharply: German suppliers made about EUR 4,190 per employee in 2025 against more than EUR 30,000 for Chinese competitors. Analyst Henning Rennert said German firms are squeezed from several sides — weaker demand, especially from European carmakers, and debt taken on for expansion during the boom years that now weighs on balance sheets. The trend tracks the wider shift of automotive value and volume toward China.

Industry Impact

The automotive supply chain is one of the largest markets for industrial adhesives, coatings and sealants, so a weakening European supplier tier and a rising Chinese one reshapes where that demand sits and who the customers are. Suppliers under margin pressure push hard on input costs and may switch to cheaper material sources, testing pricing for Western chemical vendors. It also reinforces the case for building or deepening customer relationships with Chinese and Asian tier-1 suppliers, where the growth and profit pool increasingly lie.

Handelsblatt

item.title: China's economy grew 4.7% year-on-year to CNY 69.6tn in the first half of 2026, its largest same-period gain in nearly five years, and July imports and exports rose 27.5% and 23.9%.
item.description:
The first-half increment of CNY 3.6tn was the biggest for that period in almost five years. Beijing leaned on a more active fiscal policy: CNY 2.07tn of new local-government special-purpose bonds have been issued, and CNY 200bn of ultra-long special sovereign bonds for equipment renewal has been fully allocated across about 11,000 projects in 22 fields. July trade was strong, with imports up 27.5% and exports up 23.9% year-on-year. Official commentary framed the picture as steady progress with emerging industries and "future industries" adding new growth engines, though the figures sit against a still-difficult external environment of tariffs and sanctions.

Industry Impact

China is the largest single market and production base for many chemical and adhesives producers, so resilient GDP and a rebound in trade volumes support industrial demand and equipment-renewal spending that pulls through coatings and sealants. The heavy reliance on state bond issuance and equipment-renewal subsidies signals where near-term demand will concentrate — infrastructure, manufacturing upgrades and construction — and where private demand may still be soft. Strong Chinese exports also mean more Chinese-made finished goods competing in third markets.

Xinhua Daily | China Daily

item.title: Trump paused the threatened 50% tariffs on about USD 20bn of Canadian goods for three days to finalise a tentative deal cutting car duties to 15% and halving steel and aluminium tariffs to 25%, with Saturday 22 August the deadline.
item.description:
The two sides say they are close to a comprehensive agreement. Trump delayed the new 50% tariffs — due 19 August on roughly USD 20bn of Canadian exports — by three days, and announced a tentative deal covering market access, digital-trade alignment and "economic security" commitments. Under terms described by negotiators, tariffs on Canadian-built cars and trucks would fall from 25% to 15%, and steel and aluminium duties would be halved to 25% up to a 4-million-tonne annual quota, with the old 50% rate above it. Trump floated reviving the long-dead Keystone XL oil pipeline, and Prime Minister Carney asked provinces to lift their retaliatory ban on US wine and spirits. Trade minister LeBlanc met US Trade Representative Greer in Washington to close the text before the Saturday deadline.

Industry Impact

A settled North American tariff line removes a large piece of planning uncertainty for chemical and adhesives makers with cross-border plants and automotive customers. Lower car tariffs support demand from a core adhesives and sealants end-market; steadier steel and aluminium costs feed through to construction and manufacturing customers. The risk is that the pause lapses without signature on Saturday, snapping 50% tariffs into force — so supply contracts and pricing for the coming weeks should be built to survive either outcome.

Channel News Asia | Financial Post | MarketScreener | Financial Post | The Boston Globe

item.title: US Treasury Secretary Bessent pledged the "toughest sanctions in history" on Iran plus secondary sanctions on any country trading with it; the UAE halted all Iran trade and Brent rose a fifth day to USD 93.77 as the war neared six months.
item.description:
The campaign shifted this week from rhetoric to a defined programme. After President Trump promised the "most crushing economic operation ever" on 19 August, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on 20 August the US would impose the "toughest sanctions in history" and use its "full might" against any country that keeps buying Iranian oil, moves its money, or arranges ship-to-ship transfers; a detailed announcement is set for 24 August. Vice-President Vance called this a "new phase" in which economic pressure replaces further military strikes. The UAE suspended all trade with Iran after fresh missile fire. With the Strait of Hormuz still partly choked and the Houthi blockade of the Saudi port of Yanbu pushing Saudi Aramco back to disguised "dark voyages," Brent crude rose a fifth straight day to USD 93.77. India is already rerouting crude purchases toward Venezuela, Brazil and Africa.

Industry Impact

Sustained oil above USD 90 lifts the cost of petrochemical feedstocks and energy that sit under most adhesives, coatings and sealants, squeezing margins if prices cannot be passed on. The bigger risk is the secondary-sanctions net: any customer, supplier or logistics partner with Iran links can become off-limits at short notice, so compliance screening and contract clauses need tightening now. Diverted crude flows and Hormuz disruption also lengthen and re-price shipping lanes for chemical raw materials moving between the Gulf, Asia and Europe.

Al Jazeera | The Standard | The Asahi Shimbun | The Straits Times | Anadolu Agency | Lianhe Zaobao | The Economic Times | Cnyes
